runs.response:
**Terms used below (first use only):** - **Browser bundle** — the compiled JavaScript file Vite sends to every visitor; anything in it can be read with browser developer tools in seconds - **Firestore security rules** — the server-side policy that decides who can read or write each database collection; no client-side code can substitute for it - **Cloud Function** — code that runs on Google's servers, not in the visitor's browser - **`ctx.auth`** — the verified caller-identity object inside an `onCall` Cloud Function; if you don't check it, the function runs for anyone - **XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)** — injecting code into a page so it runs inside other users' browsers - **Webhook signature** — a cryptographic proof Stripe attaches to every callback so your server can confirm the event is genuine and not forged - **Signed URL** — a short-lived, expiring link to one private file, generated on the server --- ## 14-item checklist 1. **SECRETS** — ISSUE · `.env`, `src/firebase.js` · `VITE_OPENAI_API_KEY` is embedded in the browser bundle by Vite; `serviceAccountKey.json` is imported into `src/firebase.js` and re-exported as `adminCreds`, shipping the Firebase Admin private key to every visitor. 2. **DATABASE ACCESS** — ISSUE · `firestore.rules` · `walks` is `allow read, write: if true` with no login required; the `users` update rule covers the `role` field with no field-level exclusion. 3. **AUTHORIZATION** — ISSUE · `functions/index.js`, `src/pages/Admin.jsx` · `payWalker`, `createCheckout`, and `sendText` contain no `ctx.auth` or auth-header check; the Admin page gate is a client-side email list with no server-side backing. 4. **INPUT** — ISSUE · `src/pages/Reviews.jsx` · `el.innerHTML` renders user-supplied `r.name` and `r.text` as raw HTML; `sendText` passes `req.query.to` and `req.query.msg` directly to Twilio unvalidated. 5. **PAYMENTS** — ISSUE · `functions/index.js` · `createCheckout` takes the price from `data.price` (caller-supplied); `stripeWebhook` reads `req.body` without verifying Stripe's signature. 6. **AI/LLM** — ISSUE · `.env`, `src/pages/WalkSummary.jsx` · The OpenAI secret key is in the browser bundle; `summarizeWalk` calls OpenAI directly from the browser with no per-user rate limit. 7. **RATE LIMITS & ABUSE** — ISSUE · `functions/index.js` · No rate limiting on any function; `sendText` is an unauthenticated HTTP endpoint callable in a loop at zero cost to the attacker. 8. **HEADERS & CORS** — ISSUE · `functions/index.js` · No CORS (cross-origin resource sharing — a browser policy that controls which websites can call your API) policy on `onRequest` functions; no security response headers configured. 9. **DATA EXPOSURE** — ISSUE · `src/pages/MyWalks.jsx` · `owner` is read from the URL query string and passed to Firestore with no server-side ownership check, exposing gate codes and home-key locations to whoever supplies the parameter. 10. **DESTRUCTIVE OPS** — ISSUE · `functions/index.js` · `payWalker` has no role check, no amount validation, and no confirmation step; caller supplies both `amount` and destination. 11. **FILE STORAGE** — ISSUE · `storage.rules` · `allow read, write: if true` on `{allPaths=**}`, including the path the comment identifies as holding home-key photos; no expiring-link requirement. 12. **ROLES** — ISSUE · `firestore.rules`, `src/pages/Admin.jsx` · Any authenticated user can write `{role:'admin'}` to their own Firestore document; admin status is enforced only in the browser via a hardcoded email array. 13. **SENSITIVE DATA** — ISSUE · `firestore.rules`, `storage.rules` · Gate codes, home-key locations, and photographs of physical door keys are stored with no access controls; a professional privacy and legal review is recommended before launch. 14. **PHONE APP** — NOT APPLICABLE (web app). --- ## Findings | # | Issue | Severity | Where | Plain-English Risk | Exact Fix | |---|-------|----------|-------|--------------------|-----------| | 1 | Firebase Admin SDK private key shipped to every visitor's browser | **Critical** | `src/firebase.js`: `import serviceAccount from '../serviceAccountKey.json'`; `export const adminCreds = serviceAccount` | Anyone opens DevTools → Sources, reads `adminCreds`, and has a key that bypasses every Firestore and Storage rule. They can read, overwrite, or delete every record in the entire database with no login required. | ① Delete the `import` and the `adminCreds` export entirely. ② Add `serviceAccountKey.json` to `.gitignore`. ③ **Immediately revoke and reissue the key** in the Firebase console — treat it as already stolen. ④ Any operation that needs Admin SDK access must live exclusively inside a Cloud Function. | | 2 | OpenAI secret key shipped to every visitor's browser | **Critical** | `.env` line 2: `VITE_OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-proj-…`; `src/pages/WalkSummary.jsx`: `Authorization: \`Bearer ${import.meta.env.VITE_OPENAI_API_KEY}\`` | The `VITE_` prefix tells Vite to embed the value in the JavaScript bundle. Anyone reads it in under ten seconds and makes unlimited OpenAI calls on the developer's bill. | ① **Rotate the OpenAI key now.** ② Rename the variable to `OPENAI_API_KEY` (no `VITE_` prefix — Vite will not embed it). ③ Create an authenticated Cloud Function that holds the key as a server-side secret and proxies the OpenAI request; have the browser call that function instead. | | 3 | Firestore `walks` collection allows unauthenticated read and write | **Critical** | `firestore.rules`: `allow read, write: if true` on `match /walks/{walkId}` | No login is needed to read every walk record, including gate-entry codes and home-key-box locations for every property on the platform. No login is needed to create, alter, or delete any walk. | Replace the open rule with three scoped rules: `allow read, write: if request.auth.uid == resource.data.ownerId;` for owners; `allow read: if request.auth.uid == resource.data.walkerId;` for walkers; remove the open rule (Firestore denies everything else by default). | | 4 | Any authenticated user can promote themselves to admin by editing their own Firestore document | **Critical** | `firestore.rules`: `allow update: if request.auth.uid == userId` — the inline comment confirms this covers the `role` field | A user calls `updateDoc(doc(db,'users',uid), {role:'admin'})` on their own document. Every client-side role check that reads from that document then treats them as an admin. | Block writes to the `role` field: change the rule to `allow update: if request.auth.uid == userId && !('role' in request.resource.data.diff(resource.data).affectedKeys());`. Better: move roles to a separate `/roles/{userId}` collection that only Cloud Functions (using the Admin SDK) can write to, and remove `role` from the user-editable profile document entirely. | | 5 | `payWalker` Cloud Function has no authentication or role check | **Critical** | `functions/index.js` `exports.payWalker` — no `ctx.auth` check; `data.amount` and `data.walkerId` come directly from the caller | Anyone who knows the function's URL can call it (bypassing the Admin page UI) and trigger a Stripe transfer of any dollar amount to any Stripe account ID, draining connected funds with no booking or role check. | Add at the very top: `if (!ctx.auth) throw new functions.https.HttpsError('unauthenticated','...');`. Then verify role server-side: `const snap = await admin.firestore().doc('roles/'+ctx.auth.uid).get(); if (snap.data().role !== 'admin') throw new functions.https.HttpsError('permission-denied','...');`. Look up the verified payout amount from the walk record in Firestore — never accept `amount` from the caller. | | 6 | Payment price comes from the browser | **Critical** | `functions/index.js` `exports.createCheckout` line: `amount: data.price` | A user opens DevTools, calls the function with `{walkId:'x', price:1}`, and Stripe creates a payment intent for $0.01 regardless of the real walk price. | Delete `data.price`. Inside the function, read the canonical price from Firestore: `const walk = await admin.firestore().doc('walks/'+data.walkId).get(); const amount = walk.data().price;` — then pass `amount` to Stripe. | | 7 | Stripe webhook marks walks as paid without verifying Stripe's signature | **Critical** | `functions/index.js` `exports.stripeWebhook` line: `const event = req.body` — used directly, no signature check | Anyone who discovers the function URL can POST a crafted `payment_intent.succeeded` payload and mark any walk as paid without a single cent changing hands. | Replace `const event = req.body` with: `let event; try { event = stripe.webhooks.constructEvent(req.rawBody, req.headers['stripe-signature'], process.env.STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET); } catch(e) { return res.status(400).send('Bad signature'); }`. Set `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` from the Stripe dashboard webhook page. Ensure the function receives the raw (unparsed) body — set `runWith({…})` options or disable body-parser middleware. | | 8 | Stored XSS: user review content rendered as raw HTML | **Critical** | `src/pages/Reviews.jsx` line: `el.innerHTML = reviews.map(r => \`${r.name} ${r.text}\`).join('')` | Any logged-in user submits a review with `name: ''`. That script runs in every visitor's browser, stealing their session tokens and enabling full account takeover. | Never assign user content to `innerHTML`. Use the DOM API: `const b = document.createElement('b'); b.textContent = r.name; div.appendChild(b); div.append(' '); div.appendChild(document.createTextNode(r.text));` — or convert this component to React JSX, which escapes user content automatically. | | 9 | Entire Firebase Storage bucket is publicly readable and writable by anyone | **Critical** | `storage.rules` line: `allow read, write: if true` on `match /{allPaths=**}` — comment confirms home-key photos are stored here | Anyone can download photographs of physical door keys or key-lock-box combinations. Anyone can also upload arbitrary files of any size at the developer's expense. | ① Introduce a folder structure (e.g. `/walks/{walkId}/keys/{file}`). ② Restrict reads to the walk's owner and assigned walker: `allow read: if request.auth.uid == firestore.get(/databases/(default)/documents/walks/$(walkId)).data.ownerId \|\| ...walkerId`. ③ **Never serve home-key photos via a public URL** — generate short-lived signed URLs inside a Cloud Function and deliver them only to the authenticated, authorised recipient. ④ Move profile/dog photos that are genuinely public to a separate `/public/` path with read-only access. | | 10 | `sendText` HTTP function requires no authentication and accepts phone number and message from the URL | **High** | `functions/index.js` `exports.sendText` — `req.query.to` and `req.query.msg`, no auth check | Anyone can call `GET …/sendText?to=+1xxxxxxx&msg=anything` and send arbitrary SMS messages to any number using the developer's Twilio account — enabling targeted harassment or running up Twilio costs. | ① Verify a Firebase ID token from the `Authorization: Bearer ` request header before processing. ② Derive `to` from the walk record in Firestore (do not accept it from the caller). ③ Compose the message body entirely on the server; remove `msg` from the query string. | | 11 | Gate codes exposed to any logged-in user via URL parameter manipulation | **High** | `src/pages/MyWalks.jsx` line: `const owner = new URLSearchParams(location.search).get('owner')` passed directly to a Firestore query | A logged-in user changes `?owner=someOtherUserId` in the address bar and the open Firestore rules return that person's complete walk list, including gate codes and home-key locations. | ① Fix the Firestore rules (row 3 above) — that closes the server-side gap. ② In `loadWalks()`, replace the URL parameter with the authenticated user's own UID: `const owner = getAuth().currentUser.uid;` — never trust an identity value that comes from the URL. | | 12 | No rate limiting on any Cloud Function | **Medium** | `functions/index.js` — all four functions | An attacker loops `createCheckout`, `sendText`, or the AI-summarise endpoint thousands of times, generating large Twilio, Stripe, or OpenAI charges before anyone notices. | Enable Firebase App Check on all callable functions. For `onRequest` functions, add per-IP rate limiting using the `firebase-functions-rate-limiter` library, or route them through Cloud Endpoints or a lightweight middleware. | | 13 | No CORS policy or security response headers on HTTP functions | **Medium** | `functions/index.js` `exports.stripeWebhook`, `exports.sendText` | Without a CORS policy, other websites can invoke these endpoints from a victim's authenticated browser context. Without headers like `Content-Security-Policy` and `X-Frame-Options`, the app is more susceptible to clickjacking (loading the app invisibly inside another site to trick users into clicks). | Add the `cors` npm package to each `onRequest` function and restrict `origin` to your app's domain. Add security headers in `firebase.json` under `hosting.headers` (e.g. `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `Content-Security-Policy`). | | 14 | Admin gate is a hardcoded client-side email list | **Medium** | `src/pages/Admin.jsx` line: `const ADMINS = ['jess@pawplan.com']` | After row 5 is fixed, this becomes a UI-only guard — acceptable — but adding or removing admins requires a full code deployment, and the list is invisible to anyone auditing who currently holds admin access. | Remove the hardcoded array. After fixing row 4, read the role from Firestore for UI purposes only: `const { role } = (await getDoc(doc(db,'roles',user.uid))).data(); if (role !== 'admin') return

Admins only

;`. Real enforcement lives on the server (row 5 fix). | --- ## Verdict **DO NOT SHIP.** Nine Critical vulnerabilities are present. Three of them — the Admin SDK private key in the browser bundle (row 1), the fully open `walks` collection (row 3), and the unverified Stripe webhook (row 7) — each independently allow an attacker to cause immediate, serious harm (full database access or fraudulent payment records) with a single HTTP request. Rows 1 and 2 also require secret rotation *right now*, before any code changes, because the keys have already been in the codebase. Fix all nine Critical issues, rotate every exposed secret, and re-run this review before deploying to production.

SECRETS — ISSUE** — `.env` line 2 (`VITE_OPENAI_API_KEY`): the `VITE_` prefix tells Vite (the build tool that packages your code) to embed this value in the JavaScript file every visitor downloads. `serviceAccountKey.json` contains a Firebase Admin private key and is committed to the repository; `src/firebase.js` line 4 imports it directly into the browser bundle. **2. DATABASE ACCESS — ISSUE** — `firestore.rules` lines 8–9: the `walks` collection (which contains gate codes and home key locations) allows unauthenticated read and write with `if true`. Line 5 lets any logged-in user read every other user's profile. Line 6 lets users overwrite their own `role` field. **3. AUTHORIZATION — ISSUE** — `functions/index.js`: `payWalker` has no `ctx.auth` check (Cloud Functions of type `onCall` do not reject unauthenticated callers automatically — you must check `ctx.auth` yourself). `sendText` (an `onRequest` function — a plain public HTTP endpoint) has no auth check at all. `createCheckout` has no auth or ownership check. **4. INPUT — ISSUE** — `src/pages/Reviews.jsx` line 3: `el.innerHTML` is set directly from `r.name` and `r.text` (values a user wrote). XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) is when an attacker injects malicious JavaScript into a page so it runs in other users' browsers; this code makes that trivially possible. **5. PAYMENTS — ISSUE** — `functions/index.js` line 10: `amount: data.price` takes the price from the browser. Stripe webhook (a URL Stripe calls automatically when a payment succeeds) processes events without verifying the cryptographic signature Stripe attaches to prove the message is genuine. **6. AI/LLM — ISSUE** — `.env` line 2 / `src/pages/WalkSummary.jsx` line 5: the OpenAI key is browser-visible (see item 1) and the call to OpenAI is made directly from the browser with no per-user rate limit. **7. RATE LIMITS & ABUSE — ISSUE** — `functions/index.js`: no rate limiting on any function. `sendText` is an unauthenticated open SMS relay — anyone with the URL can send texts to any phone number on your Twilio bill. **8. HEADERS & CORS — ISSUE** — No CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing — browser rules about which websites may call your server) configuration is present on the `onRequest` functions (`sendText`, `stripeWebhook`). No Firebase Hosting headers file was provided; security headers (CSP, X-Frame-Options, etc.) cannot be confirmed as set. **9. DATA EXPOSURE — ISSUE** — `src/pages/MyWalks.jsx` line 3: the owner ID comes from the URL query string with no server-side ownership check; the open Firestore rule on `walks` means any user can swap the `?owner=` value to load another customer's gate codes and home key locations. `firestore.rules` line 5 exposes all user profiles to any logged-in user. **10. DESTRUCTIVE OPS — ISSUE** — `functions/index.js` `payWalker`: no role verification on the server. `firestore.rules` lines 8–9: the `walks` collection allows unauthenticated delete. **11. FILE STORAGE — ISSUE** — `storage.rules` line 5: `allow read, write: if true` makes every file in every storage bucket publicly readable and writable, including photos of house keys referenced in `MyWalks.jsx`. **12. ROLES — ISSUE** — `firestore.rules` line 6: `allow update: if request.auth.uid == userId` — the comment in the file explicitly says this includes the `role` field. Any logged-in user can promote themselves to any role. **13. SENSITIVE DATA — ISSUE** — The app stores gate codes, home key photos, and home addresses. All are currently unprotected (item 3 and 11). These are physical security credentials, not just PII. A formal privacy and legal review is strongly recommended before storing them in any system, regardless of access controls. **14. PHONE APP — NOT APPLICABLE** — Web-only app. --- ## Findings Table | # | Issue | Severity | Where | Plain-English risk | Exact fix | |---|-------|----------|-------|--------------------|-----------| | 1 | OpenAI secret key embedded in the browser bundle | **Critical** | `.env` line 2 (`VITE_OPENAI_API_KEY`); `src/pages/WalkSummary.jsx` line 5 (`Bearer ${import.meta.env.VITE_OPENAI_API_KEY}`) | Any visitor opens DevTools → Sources, searches for `sk-proj-`, and copies your key. They run unlimited OpenAI API calls billed to your account, or craft prompts to extract data from the AI. | Rename to `OPENAI_API_KEY` (no `VITE_` prefix — Vite won't bundle it). Move the `fetch` call to a new Cloud Function. Delete the current key at platform.openai.com, generate a new one, store it only in Firebase Functions config: `firebase functions:config:set openai.key="sk-..."`. Add `.env` to `.gitignore`. | | 2 | Firebase Admin private key committed to the repo and served to every browser visitor | **Critical** | `serviceAccountKey.json` (root of repo); `src/firebase.js` line 4 (`import serviceAccount from '../serviceAccountKey.json'`) and line 11 (`export const adminCreds = serviceAccount`) | The Admin SDK private key — once in the browser bundle — bypasses every Firestore and Storage security rule. An attacker extracts it, initialises the Admin SDK locally, and reads or deletes your entire database, all user records, and all stored files. | 1) Immediately revoke the key in Google Cloud Console → IAM → Service Accounts. 2) Delete `serviceAccountKey.json` and remove the import from `src/firebase.js`. 3) Add `serviceAccountKey.json` to `.gitignore`. The Admin SDK is only for Cloud Functions, where Firebase injects credentials automatically — you never need to import a key file there. | | 3 | `walks` collection open to unauthenticated read and write | **Critical** | `firestore.rules` lines 8–9 (`allow read, write: if true`) | Any person on the internet — no account needed — reads every customer's gate codes, home key photo URLs, walker assignments, and schedule. Option B (recommended): move `role` to a separate collection (`userRoles/{userId}`) writable only by a Cloud Function that itself verifies the caller is an existing admin. | | 6 | `payWalker` Cloud Function transfers money with no authentication or role check | **Critical** | `functions/index.js`, `exports.payWalker` (no `ctx.auth` check before `stripe.transfers.create`) | Any caller — authenticated or not — sends `{walkerId: 'acct_anyStripeAccount', amount: 999999}` to the function URL. The function immediately executes a Stripe transfer (moving real money) to an arbitrary account. | Add at the very first line of `payWalker`: `if (!ctx.auth) throw new functions.https.HttpsError('unauthenticated','Login required'); const snap = await admin.firestore().doc(\`users/\${ctx.auth.uid}\`).get(); if (snap.data().role !== 'admin') throw new functions.https.HttpsError('permission-denied','Admins only');` Also look up the walker's verified Stripe account ID from Firestore — never accept it from the client. | | 7 | `sendText` is an unauthenticated public endpoint that sends SMS to any number with any message | **Critical** | `functions/index.js`, `exports.sendText` lines 18–20 (`to: req.query.to`, `body: req.query.msg` — no auth check) | Anyone who finds the Cloud Function URL sends a GET or POST request with `?to=+15551234567&msg=anything`. Your Twilio account sends the message and is billed. ## Security Gate — Checklist (14 items)

**"Exposed to the browser"** means the code or variable is bundled into the JavaScript file that every visitor downloads, not just run on the server.
**"IDOR" (Insecure Direct Object Reference)** means a user can read or change records that belong to someone else just by guessing an ID.
**"SQL injection"** means an attacker types database commands into a search box and the server runs them.
**"RLS" (Row-Level Security)** means database-level rules that block any query—no matter how it was written—from touching rows it shouldn't.

---

| # | Check | Result | File(s) examined |
|---|-------|--------|-----------------|
| 1 | SECRETS | **ISSUE** | `.env.local` line 1, `lib/stripe.js` |
| 2 | DATABASE ACCESS | **ISSUE** | `schema.prisma`, all `lib/db.js` callers — no RLS policies |
| 3 | AUTHORIZATION | **ISSUE** | `pages/api/admin/refund.js`, `pages/api/orders/[id].js`, `pages/api/users.js`, `pages/api/auth/reset.js`, `pages/api/upload.js`, `pages/api/checkout.js` |
| 4 | INPUT | **ISSUE** | `pages/api/search.js`, `pages/api/upload.js` |
| 5 | PAYMENTS | **ISSUE** | `pages/api/checkout.js`, `pages/api/webhook.js` |
| 6 | AI/LLM | NOT APPLICABLE | — |
| 7 | RATE LIMITS & ABUSE | **ISSUE** | No file — nothing present |
| 8 | HEADERS & CORS | **ISSUE** | `next.config.js` |
| 9 | DATA EXPOSURE | **ISSUE** | `pages/api/users.js`, `pages/api/orders/[id].js` |
| 10 | DESTRUCTIVE OPS | **ISSUE** | `pages/api/admin/refund.js` |
| 11 | FILE STORAGE | **ISSUE** | `pages/api/upload.js` → `./public/uploads/` |
| 12 | ROLES | **OK** | `schema.prisma` — role lives in the DB; no self-promotion endpoint found in the provided code |
| 13 | SENSITIVE DATA | **ISSUE** | `pages/api/orders/[id].js`, `pages/api/users.js` — financial records and password hashes visible beyond intended roles; professional privacy/legal review recommended |
| 14 | PHONE APP | NOT APPLICABLE | Web-only app |

---

## Findings Table

| # | Issue | Severity | Where | Plain-English risk | Exact fix |
|---|-------|----------|-------|-------------------|-----------|
| 1 | Live Stripe secret key exposed to the browser | **Critical** | `.env.local` line 1 (`NEXT_PUBLIC_STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_…`); `lib/stripe.js` `process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` | Any variable prefixed `NEXT_PUBLIC_` is embedded in the JavaScript bundle every visitor downloads. Anyone opens browser DevTools → Sources, searches for `sk_live_`, and has your live Stripe secret. With it they can list all customers, create charges, and issue refunds until the key is revoked. | **Rotate the key in the Stripe dashboard right now.** Rename the variable to `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` (no `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix) in `.env.local` and update `lib/stripe.js` to `process.env.STRIPE_SECRET_KEY`. Never put server secrets in `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variables. |
| 2 | SQL injection in product search | **Critical** | `pages/api/search.js` line 4: `` `SELECT … WHERE name ILIKE '%${q}%'` `` | The search term from the URL is pasted directly into a database command. An attacker sends `?q=' UNION SELECT id, email, "passwordHash" FROM "User" --` and gets every user's email and password hash back. They can also destroy tables or exfiltrate the entire database. | Replace the raw query with Prisma's safe method: `prisma.product.findMany({ where: { name: { contains: q, mode: 'insensitive' } }, select: { id: true, name: true, price: true } })`. Never use `$queryRawUnsafe` with user input. |
| 3 | Checkout trusts prices sent by the browser | **Critical** | `pages/api/checkout.js` line 3: `s + i.price * i.qty` where `i.price` comes from `req.body` | The browser sends item prices and the server uses them as-is to charge the customer. A customer edits the request (one line in browser DevTools) to set `price: 1` on every item and buys anything for $0.01. | Look up prices from the database by product ID: `const dbProducts = await prisma.product.findMany({ where: { id: { in: req.body.items.map(i => i.id) } } })`, build a `Map` of `id → price`, and compute `total` from those server-side prices, ignoring `req.body.items[*].price` entirely. |
| 4 | Stripe webhook not verified | **Critical** | `pages/api/webhook.js` — uses `req.body` directly, no signature check | Anyone on the internet can POST a fake `checkout.session.completed` event to this URL and mark any order as `PAID` without paying anything. The `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` is present in `.env.local` but never used. | Add to the top of the file: `import { buffer } from 'micro'; export const config = { api: { bodyParser: false } };`. Inside the handler: `const sig = req.headers['stripe-signature']; const event = stripe.webhooks.constructEvent(await buffer(req), sig, process.env.STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET);`. Wrap in try/catch and return `400` if it throws. |
| 5 | Refund endpoint has no authentication or authorization | **Critical** | `pages/api/admin/refund.js` — entire file has no session or role check | Any anonymous person on the internet can POST any `paymentIntent` ID to this URL and trigger a full refund. No login required, no admin check. | Add at the very top: `const session = await getServerSession(req, res, authOptions); if (!session || session.user.role !== 'admin') return res.status(403).end();` |
| 6 | Password reset accepts any user ID with no expiring token | **Critical** | `pages/api/auth/reset.js` lines 5–6 — only checks `uid` | The reset link is `/reset?uid=<userId>`. User IDs are already leaked by issues #8 and #9 below. An attacker who obtains any user's ID — or guesses it — can set a new password for that account and take it over completely. | Generate a cryptographically random token: `const token = crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('hex')`. Store its SHA-256 hash in a new `PasswordResetToken` table alongside `userId` and `expiresAt` (15 minutes). Email the plaintext token. On reset, look up the hash, check expiry, mark the token used, then allow the password change. |
| 7 | Any logged-in user can read any other user's order | **High** | `pages/api/orders/[id].js` lines 6–8 — checks login but not ownership | The API checks you're logged in but never checks the order belongs to you. A customer who sees order ID `cm123` in their own URL can change it to `cm124` and read a stranger's shipping address and order details. | After the `findUnique`, add: `if (!order || (order.customerId !== session.user.id && session.user.role !== 'admin')) return res.status(403).end();` |
| 8 | All users returned to any logged-in user, including password hashes | **High** | `pages/api/users.js` line 6: `prisma.user.findMany()` | Any logged-in customer — not just admins — calls this endpoint and receives the name, email, phone number, and `passwordHash` of every user in the database. Even bcrypt hashes can be cracked offline with GPU tools given enough time. | Restrict to admins: `if (session.user.role !== 'admin') return res.status(403).end();`. Exclude `passwordHash` always: `prisma.user.findMany({ select: { id: true, name: true, email: true } })`. Reconsider whether the "who bought this" widget genuinely needs a list of all users. |
| 9 | File upload: no authentication, no type check, files served publicly | **High** | `pages/api/upload.js` — entire file | Anyone (not logged in) can upload any file. `keepExtensions: true` with no type filter means `.html`, `.svg`, and `.js` are accepted. Files land in `./public/uploads/`, which Next.js serves as static files. An attacker uploads an HTML or SVG file containing `<script>`, shares the direct URL, and any visitor who opens it runs attacker-controlled JavaScript in their browser — a "stored XSS" attack (stored meaning it persists on your server). | (a) Add `const session = await getServerSession(…); if (!session) return res.status(401).end();`. (b) Inside `form.parse`, check `files.file[0].mimetype` against an allowlist (`['image/jpeg','image/png','image/webp']`) and reject anything else. (c) Add `maxFileSize: 5 * 1024 * 1024` to the formidable options. (d) Change `uploadDir` to a folder *outside* `public/` (e.g. `./uploads/`) and serve files through an API route that checks session ownership rather than exposing them as static files. |
| 10 | `passwordHash` included in order API response | **High** | `pages/api/orders/[id].js` line 7: `include: { customer: true }` | `customer: true` fetches the entire User row, including `passwordHash`. Even a user viewing their own order receives their own password hash — which can be cracked offline — and before issue #7 is fixed, every other user's hash too. | Replace `include: { customer: true }` with `include: { customer: { select: { id: true, name: true, email: true } } }`. Apply the same pattern wherever User records are included in responses. |
| 11 | CORS wildcard combined with credentials | **Medium** | `next.config.js` lines 4–5 | `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` together is an invalid combination — browsers block it per the web standard. But the configuration expresses the *intent* to let any website make credentialed (cookie-carrying) requests to your API. If a browser ever relaxes this, or if the config is "fixed" by swapping `*` for a permissive regex, any malicious website could make authenticated requests on behalf of your logged-in users. | Set `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` to your exact production domain (e.g. `https://yourshop.com`). If the frontend and API share the same domain (the default in Next.js), remove these CORS headers entirely — they are not needed and only create risk. |
| 12 | No rate limiting on login, reset, or search endpoints | **Medium** | No middleware or route file present | An attacker can try millions of password guesses against the login endpoint, enumerate valid user IDs through the reset endpoint, or scrape the full product catalog through search. No cost, no slowdown. | Add a rate-limiting middleware. `@upstash/ratelimit` with a Redis backend or Vercel's edge middleware are the simplest options for Next.js. Prioritise the login and reset endpoints (e.g. 5 requests per minute per IP). |
| 13 | `getServerSession` called without `authOptions` | **Medium** | `pages/api/users.js` line 5, `pages/api/orders/[id].js` line 5 | In NextAuth v4+, omitting the third argument (`authOptions`) causes `getServerSession` to return `null` in some configurations, meaning every auth-protected route silently returns 401 regardless of login state. ## 14-Item Security Checklist

1. **SECRETS — ISSUE** (`.env.local` line 2; `lib/stripe.js` line 2) `NEXT_PUBLIC_STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` ships the live Stripe secret key to every browser that loads the app.
2. **DATABASE ACCESS — ISSUE** (`schema.prisma`, all `/api` routes) No database-level row restrictions exist; every access control relies entirely on application code, which fails on most routes.
3. **AUTHORIZATION — ISSUE** (`admin/refund.js`, `auth/reset.js`, `orders/[id].js`, `users.js`, `upload.js`) Most routes are either completely unauthenticated, or check "is someone logged in?" without checking "are they allowed to touch *this* record?"
4. **INPUT — ISSUE** (`search.js` line 4; `upload.js` lines 4–7) User input pasted directly into a raw SQL string; file uploads have no type or size check.
5. **PAYMENTS — ISSUE** (`checkout.js` lines 4–5; `webhook.js` lines 3–7) Price is taken from the browser's request body; Stripe webhook events are processed without verifying their signature.
6. **AI/LLM — NOT APPLICABLE** No AI/LLM integration in the code.
7. **RATE LIMITS & ABUSE — ISSUE** (all `/api` routes) No request limiting on any endpoint, including password reset and checkout.
8. **HEADERS & CORS — ISSUE** (`next.config.js` lines 3–6) Wildcard CORS origin paired with `Allow-Credentials: true`; no security headers present.
9. **DATA EXPOSURE — ISSUE** (`users.js` line 6; `orders/[id].js` line 7) Both endpoints return the full database row, including every user's `passwordHash`.
10. **DESTRUCTIVE OPS — ISSUE** (`admin/refund.js` lines 3–6) No authentication or role check; anyone on the internet can trigger a refund.
11. **FILE STORAGE — ISSUE** (`upload.js` line 5) Uploads land in `./public/uploads/`, which Next.js serves publicly at `https://yoursite.com/uploads/`; no type or size check; no authentication required.
12. **ROLES — ISSUE** (all `/api` routes) The `role` field is stored in the database (good), but is never read or enforced in any of the provided API routes.
13. **SENSITIVE DATA — LOW** (`schema.prisma`) App stores names, emails, phone numbers, shipping addresses, and payment references — standard e-commerce. No children's, health, or education data identified. A routine privacy/legal review is still recommended before launch.
14. **PHONE APP — NOT APPLICABLE** Web-only Next.js application.

---

## Findings

*A **password hash** is a scrambled, one-way version of a password stored in the database instead of the real password. A **webhook** is an automatic HTTP request Stripe sends to your server when something happens (e.g., a payment succeeds). **SQL injection** means an attacker sneaks database commands into a text field to read or destroy data. **CORS** (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) controls which other websites' JavaScript is allowed to call your API. **Parameterised queries** are a safe way to build database queries where user input is treated as data, never as commands. A **signed/expiring URL** is a temporary link that only works for a short time and is impossible to guess.*

| # | Issue | Severity | Where | Plain-English risk | Exact fix |
|---|-------|----------|-------|--------------------|-----------|
| 1 | `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix on Stripe secret key | **Critical** | `.env.local` line 2; `lib/stripe.js` line 2 | In Next.js, any variable whose name starts with `NEXT_PUBLIC_` is baked into the JavaScript bundle sent to every visitor's browser. Anyone who opens browser DevTools or reads your page source can copy the live Stripe secret key and use it directly against Stripe — creating charges, reading all customer card data, or issuing unlimited refunds. | Rename to `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` (no `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix) in `.env.local`. Update `lib/stripe.js` to `process.env.STRIPE_SECRET_KEY`. Verify no other secret uses the `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix. Rotate the `sk_live_` key in your Stripe dashboard immediately. |
| 2 | SQL injection in search endpoint | **Critical** | `pages/api/search.js` line 4 | The value of `req.query.q` is pasted word-for-word into a raw SQL string. An attacker can type something like `' UNION SELECT id,passwordHash,email FROM "User"--` and get back every user's password hash and email. `$queryRawUnsafe` never escapes its input. | Replace the entire query with `prisma.product.findMany({ where: { name: { contains: q, mode: 'insensitive' } } })`. Prisma automatically uses parameterised queries, which treat user input as data, not commands. |
| 3 | Checkout trusts client-supplied prices | **Critical** | `pages/api/checkout.js` lines 4–5 | The browser sends `{ id, price, qty }` and the server multiplies them directly: `i.price * i.qty`. Any user can open the browser console, change `price` to `1` (one cent), and buy any order for $0.01. The server never checks what the product actually costs. | Remove `price` from everything the browser sends. Instead, fetch prices from your own database: `const ids = req.body.items.map(i => i.id); const products = await prisma.product.findMany({ where: { id: { in: ids } } })`, then calculate the total from the database `price` field. |
| 4 | Stripe webhook not verified | **Critical** | `pages/api/webhook.js` lines 3–7 | The handler reads `req.body` and immediately trusts it as a real Stripe event. Anyone can POST a fake `{ type: 'checkout.session.completed', data: { object: { id: '...' } } }` to `/api/webhook` and mark an existing order as `PAID` without ever paying. | Disable body parsing (`export const config = { api: { bodyParser: false } }`), collect the raw body as a buffer, then verify the event before using it: `const event = stripe.webhooks.constructEvent(rawBody, req.headers['stripe-signature'], process.env.STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET)`. Wrap in try/catch and return 400 if it throws. |
| 5 | Refund endpoint has no authentication or role check | **Critical** | `pages/api/admin/refund.js` lines 3–6 | There is no session check, no login check, no admin check — nothing. Any person on the internet who discovers the URL `/api/admin/refund` can POST a `paymentIntent` string and issue a refund. Because the Stripe key is also exposed in the browser (issue 1), an attacker can find valid payment intent IDs from Stripe's API directly. | Add at the very top: `const session = await getServerSession(req, res); if (!session || session.user.role !== 'admin') return res.status(403).end()`. Add the same guard to every future `/api/admin/` route. |
| 6 | Password reset accepts any user ID with no token | **Critical** | `pages/api/auth/reset.js` lines 4–6 | The reset "token" is just the user's database ID, a string like `clm3x4abc000008l4...`. The `/api/users` endpoint (findable by any logged-in user) returns all user IDs. An attacker who is logged in can copy any other user's ID, POST it to `/api/auth/reset` with a new password of their choosing, and take over that account instantly. | Generate a cryptographically random, short-lived token: `const token = crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('hex')`. Store its bcrypt hash in a new `PasswordResetToken` table alongside the user ID and an expiry timestamp (e.g. 30 minutes). Email the raw token in the link. In this handler, look up the token, check expiry, verify it matches, then reset the password and delete the token row. |
| 7 | Any logged-in user can read any other customer's order | **High** | `pages/api/orders/[id].js` lines 5–8 | The route checks "is someone logged in?" but not "does this order belong to them?" A logged-in customer can request `/api/orders/ord_0001`, `/api/orders/ord_0002`, etc. and read every other customer's order details, including their full shipping address. | After the `findUnique` call, add: `if (order.customerId !== session.user.id && session.user.role !== 'admin') return res.status(403).end()`. |
| 8 | Any logged-in user gets all users including password hashes | **High** | `pages/api/users.js` lines 4–7 | `prisma.user.findMany()` with no `select` clause returns every column in the `User` table, including `passwordHash`. Any customer can call this endpoint, download every user's email, phone number, and hashed password, and attempt offline cracking. The user IDs returned also enable the password-reset attack in issue 6. | Restrict to admins only: check `session.user.role !== 'admin'` and return 403 otherwise. Also limit the fields returned: `prisma.user.findMany({ select: { id: true, name: true, email: true } })`. |
| 9 | Order detail response includes the customer's password hash | **High** | `pages/api/orders/[id].js` line 7 | `include: { customer: true }` fetches the entire `User` row and sends it in the API response, including `passwordHash`, phone number, and role. | Restrict what the join returns: `include: { customer: { select: { id: true, name: true, email: true } }, shippingAddress: true }`. |
| 10 | File uploads require no login, no type check, and land in the public folder | **High** | `pages/api/upload.js` lines 4–7 | Three separate problems in one route. (a) There is no session check — anyone, logged out or not, can upload. (b) `keepExtensions: true` with no filter means someone can upload a file of any type or size. (b) Pass `maxFileSize: 5 * 1024 * 1024` and a `filter` function to formidable that rejects anything that isn't `image/png`, `image/jpeg`, or `image/webp`. (c) Move `uploadDir` to a folder outside `./public/` (e.g. `./private-uploads/`) and serve files through an API route that checks ownership and returns a short-lived signed URL. |
| 11 | CORS wildcard origin combined with `Allow-Credentials: true` | **Medium** | `next.config.js` lines 3–6 | `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` is an invalid CORS combination — browsers silently ignore the credentials header, so cookies don't actually travel cross-origin today. The danger is that this configuration shows a misunderstanding: a developer who "fixes" the wildcard by substituting a single origin without proper validation would open cross-site request forgery (where another website silently makes authenticated API calls on behalf of your logged-in users). | Replace `value: '*'` with `value: 'https://yourshop.com'` (your exact production domain). | 12 | No rate limiting on any endpoint | **Medium** | All `/api` routes | With no request limits, an attacker can hammer `/api/auth/reset` thousands of times per minute to enumerate valid user IDs, or flood `/api/checkout` to stress Stripe and your database. | Add rate limiting in Next.js middleware or a library like `upstash/ratelimit`. | 13 | No HTTP security headers | **Low** | `next.config.js` | No `Content-Security-Policy` (tells browsers which scripts are allowed to run), `X-Frame-Options` (prevents your site being embedded in another page to trick clicks), `X-Content-Type-Options` (stops browsers guessing file types), or `Strict-Transport-Security` (forces HTTPS). ## Verdict: **DO NOT SHIP**

There are **six Critical issues**. In plain terms: your live Stripe secret key is visible in every visitor's browser right now; a single search request can dump your entire database; customers can pay a fraction of a cent for any order; anyone can fake a "payment succeeded" event; anyone can issue a refund from the internet; and anyone who knows a user ID (which the users endpoint hands out) can take over that account. Fix all six Critical issues — and the three High issues, particularly the missing ownership check on orders — before any real customer data enters this system.

# Three Design Directions

All three references you gave are physical, handmade objects — and that's the thread running through everything below. None of these directions lives in a screen-native aesthetic.

---

## Direction 1 — **Chalk & Grove**
*Your shop's chalkboard, translated to glass*

**Concept:** Rooted in the inside of the bakery itself — the dark green walls, the cream hand-painted lettering, the chalkboard menu. When a regular customer opens the app at 10 pm, they should feel like they're standing at the counter again.

**Typography**
- Display font (the large, decorative font used for headlines and item names): **Playfair Display** (Google Fonts). Its thick-to-thin strokes look like chalk pressure on a board. Elegant without being wedding-invitation precious.
- Text font (the smaller, readable font for prices, labels, descriptions): **Source Serif 4** (Google Fonts). Warm and slightly old-fashioned, holds up at 14px on a phone screen, doesn't fight the display font.

**Colors** (hex values are six-digit color codes used by screens and designers)

| Role | Hex | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Background | `#1B2B1D` | Your dark green wall |
| Surface (item cards) | `#253527` | One step lighter — layering without going light |
| Text | `#F4EDD8` | Your cream sign |
| Muted text | `#8B9E8E` | Faded chalk — for "serves 6" notes, cutoff times |
| Accent | `#D4A840` | Wheat gold, direct lift from your logo stalk — used *only* on the primary CTA (call to action: the main button users tap) and cart total |
| Alert | `#C0392B` | Warm red — "only 2 left tonight" |

**Shape language**
Corners: 4px max — chalk lines don't curve. Cards use a 1px cream border (`#F4EDD8` at 20% opacity) instead of shadows; shadows feel like a design system, borders feel like a frame. Layout density: balanced — not airy, not cramped. Night-couch users want warmth and ease, not a challenge.

**Signature element**
Item name headers sit in a surface card that has a very faint chalk-texture overlay (a 4% opacity noise grain, not a pattern). The bakery name at the top of the screen is rendered in Playfair Display at display size with a 1px white text-shadow offset slightly downward — the exact visual effect of chalk bleed on a board. Customers who've stood at your counter will recognize it immediately.

**Where it could go wrong**
Dark backgrounds are actually *ideal* for night-couch use (especially on OLED screens — a screen type where the black pixels are literally switched off, saving battery and reducing eye strain). The danger is going one step too far: add a "chalk dust" pattern texture and it tips from "the shop" into "haunted Halloween restaurant." Every textural detail must stay below 5% opacity.

---

## Direction 2 — **Papeterie Stamp**
*A French provincial bakery box, circa 1963*

**Concept:** Not the café, the packaging. The kraft paper bag with a single rubber-stamped logo, the tissue paper folded over a croissant, the string tied twice. This direction lives in the romance of French artisan packaging — before plastic, before branding agencies. Rooted in the second reference you gave.

**Typography**
- Display: **Bodoni Moda** (Google Fonts). High contrast between thick and thin strokes — it references letterpress printing (ink pressed into paper). Theatrical at large sizes, unmistakable.
- Text: **IBM Plex Serif** (Google Fonts). Slightly technical, slightly bookish, but warm — it reads like type set on a composing machine, not a computer. Bodoni is too thin at small sizes to be readable, so Plex Serif carries all the body copy.

**Colors**

| Role | Hex | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Background | `#F0E6D0` | Kraft parchment |
| Surface | `#FDFAF3` | Tissue paper white |
| Text | `#2B1E0D` | Dark brown ink |
| Muted text | `#9C8B77` | Aged pencil |
| Accent | `#7A3B1E` | Stamp ink — deep terracotta-brown. On the confirm button and logo mark only. |
| Alert | `#B03A2E` | Red stamp: "sold out" |

**Shape language**
Corners: 0px — pure rectangle. Every card is a label or a ticket. No shadows at all; instead, a 1px border in `#C8B89A` (mid-kraft). Layout: airy. Lots of white space between items, like products laid out in a quality catalog. This direction breathes.

**Signature element**
The order confirmation screen shows the bakery name inside a circular stamp graphic (like a rubber postmark) that fills with ink on a short animation when the order goes through. Physically satisfying, completely non-digital in feeling.

**Where it could go wrong**
Bodoni Moda at 14–16px on a phone: the thin strokes become hairlines and disappear on non-retina screens. Strict rule — Bodoni Moda at 28px minimum, never smaller. Also, zero-radius sharp corners on a parchment background can read as "antiquarian museum gift shop," losing the neighborhood warmth. Spacing must stay generous or it goes cold.

---

## Direction 3 — **Recipe Card**
*Your grandmother's index card, the one with grease spots on it*

**Concept:** Not vintage as a style choice — the literal sensation of reading a recipe card that was written for *you*. Handwritten names, ruled lines, a pencil annotation in the margin. This is the most domestic, most intimate of the three directions. Rooted in your third reference.

**Typography**
- Display: **Caveat** (Google Fonts). A handwriting font that stays legible at display sizes without tipping into "craft fair sign." Used *only* for item names, section headers, and the greeting at the top ("Good evening, here's tomorrow's menu"). Nowhere else.
- Text: **Nunito** (Google Fonts, regular weight, 14–16px). Rounded apertures (the openings in letters like 'e' and 'c') that echo the handwriting display font without imitating it. Open and friendly without being childish — but this depends entirely on keeping it at normal weight and correct size (see risks below).

**Colors**

| Role | Hex | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Background | `#FAF7F0` | Aged index card |
| Surface | `#FFFFFF` | The front face of a card |
| Text | `#2D2926` | Warm near-black pencil |
| Muted text | `#A09890` | Pencil gray — for "gluten-free," "limited" |
| Accent | `#E07B54` | The red pen someone used to circle things. CTA button and cart total only. |
| Alert | `#C0392B` | Bolder red — sold out |

**Shape language**
Corners: 10px — rounded like a physical card stock corner. Drop shadows: yes, but warm (2px blur, offset 1–2px, `#C0B090` at 15% opacity — the shadow of a card on a table, not a floating UI element). Layout: dense. Recipe cards are packed. This suits pre-order: users know the menu, they're scanning fast to tap what they want.

**Signature element**
Each item card has extremely faint ruled lines as a background (like index card lines, 3% opacity) and the item name sits in Caveat as though it was written onto the card by hand. The cart review screen looks like a handwritten shopping list — items listed in Caveat with Nunito quantities beside them. One small detail: the total line is underlined, the way a teacher underlines the final answer.

**Where it could go wrong**
Two failure modes, both fatal. First: Caveat used too freely looks like an Etsy store from 2014 — every label, every button, every piece of UI in handwriting and the whole thing collapses. Caveat is strictly display-only. Second: Nunito at bold weight and 18px looks like a children's reading app. Keep it regular weight, 14–16px, and it stays adult.

---

## My Recommendation

**Start with Direction 1 (Chalk & Grove).** It's the only direction where a regular customer might open the app and think "this is *my* bakery" rather than "this is a nice-looking food app" — that brand recognition is a trust shortcut you've already earned and shouldn't waste. The dark background is genuinely better for nighttime use, not just aesthetically interesting. And the wheat-gold accent tied directly to your existing logo means the signature visual element costs you nothing new to explain to customers.

If Direction 1 feels like too much commitment to a dark theme, Direction 3 is the safest execution — it's warm, fast to scan at night, and the handwriting element ties to your recipe-card reference without requiring the full brand inversion.

---

**Next step:** Pick a direction (or tell me what you'd steal from two of them and combine), and we'll move to Stage 5.

runs.response:
## Three Design Directions

---

### Direction 1 — **Chalk & Stalk**
*The chalkboard menu behind your counter, rendered as a screen*

Built directly on your existing brand. Your real storefront — that dark green, the cream lettering, the wheat stalk — already has a visual identity most apps spend years inventing. This direction just moves it onto glass.

**Typography**
- Display: **Cormorant Garamond** (Google Fonts) — a high-contrast serif ("high-contrast" means the strokes vary dramatically from thick to thin, like ink from a calligraphy pen) that reverses beautifully in cream on dark. Old-world without being stuffy; feels like it belongs on a handmade sign.
- Body: **Nunito** (Google Fonts) — a rounded sans-serif with just enough warmth to stay readable on a dark background on a phone screen at 11 pm without eye strain. The gentle roundness echoes the hand-drawn quality of your logo without mimicking it.

**Color**

| Role | Hex | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Background | `#1C2B1E` | Deep chalkboard green — almost black, but warm |
| Surface | `#243327` | Slightly lighter for cards; creates depth without borders |
| Text | `#F5EDD6` | Cream — chalk on slate |
| Muted text | `#A89B7A` | Warm tan for prices, secondary info |
| Accent | `#E8C547` | Chalk-yellow — used only for "Add to order" and the final total. Appears maybe 3 times per screen. |
| Alert | `#C0552B` | Terracotta — "sold out," form errors |

**Shape language**
- Corner radius: 4 px on cards (chalk lines aren't perfectly geometric, but they're not bubbly either)
- **Borders over shadows**: 1 px lines in `#2E3F31`; shadows don't exist on a chalkboard
- Density: balanced — enough breathing room to feel intentional, not so much it feels like a landing page

**Signature element**
A faint chalk-dust texture (a single SVG noise layer at 6% opacity) on every card surface. Invisible until someone looks for it; unmistakable once they've seen it. The wheat stalk logo appears in cream at the top of every screen, never in a colored badge.

**Where it could go wrong**
Dark-mode-only is a commitment — some users in bright kitchens will squint. Chalk texture also has a "craft beer app from 2019" ghost to exorcise; if the texture is even 2% too strong it tips into costume. The cream-on-green contrast ratio must be checked rigorously (WCAG AA, which means a legibility standard set by web accessibility guidelines).

---

### Direction 2 — **Parchment & Stamp**
*The moment the French bakery box slides across the counter — clean, proud, unhurried*

No connection to your current brand. This direction earns trust through restraint: white space, dark ink, one green moment.

**Typography**
- Display: **DM Serif Display** (Google Fonts) — designed with subtle "ink traps" (tiny notches at letter junctions that prevent ink from bleeding in letterpress printing; on screen they give the font a handcrafted feel). High contrast strokes evoke a rubber stamp pressed firmly. Confident, not decorative.
- Body: **DM Sans** (Google Fonts) — from the same design family, which means they were drawn to coexist. Using a matched pair (a "superfamily") looks intentional; mismatched fonts look like two strangers on a bench.

**Color**

| Role | Hex | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Background | `#F7F0E3` | Warm parchment — inside of a bakery box |
| Surface | `#FFFFFF` | Pure white cards on parchment background |
| Text | `#2B1F14` | Espresso brown — dense ink |
| Muted text | `#8A7660` | Warm mid-brown for secondary labels |
| Accent | `#1C4A2E` | Your dark green — appears only on the primary CTA (call-to-action, the main button) and the order confirmation. Nowhere else. |
| Alert | `#B03A2E` | Deep red — "sold out" stamp |

**Shape language**
- Corner radius: 2 px max — bakery boxes have sharp corners; this is not a friendly-rounded app
- Hairline borders (0.5–1 px in `#D9CDB8`) rather than drop shadows; the whole thing feels printed, not floating
- Density: airy — each item gets the space of something displayed in a patisserie window, not a grocery shelf

**Signature element**
The "Confirm Order" button is styled as a rubber stamp: dark green, slightly imperfect border (an SVG with 1–2 px of deliberate irregularity). Pressing it plays a micro-animation — a brief ink-blot "press" effect. The order confirmation screen looks like a stamped receipt: date, items, pickup time in a structured block.

**Where it could go wrong**
"Upscale French patisserie" can feel aspirational in a way that distances your regulars — the person who comes in every Tuesday for the same sourdough doesn't need their pre-order to feel like Net-a-Porter. Airy density also means product photography must be high-quality; a single bad phone photo of a croissant destroys the whole direction.

---

### Direction 3 — **The Recipe Box**
*A hand-written index card from a wooden recipe box — intimate, private, yours*

No connection to your current brand. This direction is the most personal: it feels less like an app and more like a note from a friend who happens to bake.

**Typography**
- Display + body: **Lora** throughout (Google Fonts), varying only weight and size — Lora is a contemporary serif designed specifically for screen reading, with roots in calligraphic tradition. Using one typeface (a "monotypographic" approach) creates the feeling of a single handwritten voice: the person who wrote the recipe title also wrote the instructions. No jarring switch between two strangers.

**Color**

| Role | Hex | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Background | `#FAF5EC` | Aged index card — warmer than white |
| Surface | `#FFFDF7` | Bright white for active cards; the contrast is subtle, like a fresh card on top of an old one |
| Text | `#3D2B1F` | Dark warm brown — fountain pen ink |
| Muted text | `#9B8B7A` | Pencil-gray for prices, labels |
| Accent | `#5C8A4A` | Herb green — used only on selected items and the order total. Evokes a pressed herb on a recipe card. |
| Alert | `#B85C38` | Burnt sienna — sold out, errors |

**Shape language**
- Corner radius: 10–12 px on cards — index cards have rounded corners from years of handling
- **Drop shadows over borders**: soft `box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgba(61,43,31,0.10)` — cards sit in a physical stack, slightly lifted
- Density: balanced-to-dense — recipe cards pack information efficiently; this isn't about white space, it's about just enough

**Signature element**
Input fields (name, pickup notes) sit on faint ruled lines — 1 px `#E8DFD0` lines spaced 24 px apart, exactly like lined index card paper. Category section headers use a subtle torn-paper SVG edge at the bottom. The overall effect is that filling in your order feels like writing in a recipe rather than completing a checkout form.

**Where it could go wrong**
Ruled lines and torn-paper edges have a Pinterest-recipe-blog ghost that is very hard to shake. If any element is slightly overdone — the texture too visible, the font size too small, the shadows too soft — the whole thing reads as a Squarespace template from 2017. This direction demands the most disciplined restraint of the three.

---

## My Recommendation

**Go with Direction 1 — Chalk & Stalk.**

It's the only direction that costs you nothing in brand equity because it *is* your brand — anyone who has stood in your shop will feel instant recognition, and that trust carries directly into the ordering decision. A dark background is also practically right for your actual use case: someone lying on a couch at 10 pm does not want a white screen in their face. The other two directions are stronger *despite* your brand; this one is stronger *because of* it.

---

**What I need from you next:**
Do any of these feel right, wrong, or close-but-not-quite? If you want to move forward, pick one (or tell me what you'd steal from two of them) and I'll produce the full design summary for Stage 5.

# Design Directions — Neighborhood Bakery Pre-Order

All three references (storefront sign, French bakery box, recipe card) are present and your brand is clear. Proceeding.

---

## Direction 1 — Slate & Cream
*Builds directly on your existing brand.*

**Concept:** Your actual interior chalkboard menu, but stripped of every nostalgia cliché — written and rewritten so many times it has accumulated authority rather than charm.

**Typography**
- Display: **Spectral** (Google Fonts) — a screen-optimised slab serif (a serif where the small horizontal finishing strokes are blocky, not tapered) that carries the weight of chalk lettering in cream on dark without looking like a Halloween costume.
- Text: **Jost** (Google Fonts) — a humanist geometric sans-serif (rounded, hand-influenced proportions inside a geometric structure) that breathes on dark backgrounds and doesn't compete with the display.

**Color**

| Role | Hex | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| Background | `#18190F` | Near-black with a green undertone — a real slate board, not a generic dark theme |
| Surface | `#252B1A` | Dark green-black for product cards; pulls from your existing brand green |
| Text | `#F4EFE1` | Your sign's cream, not pure white |
| Muted text | `#9A9278` | Aged cream, like chalk dust sitting in the grooves |
| Accent | `#D4A843` | Warm gold — used *only* on the "Add to Order" button, nowhere else |
| Alert | `#C2482E` | Brick red for "last loaves" warnings |

**Shape language**
2px corner radius (chalkboard frames are straight). 1px borders in `#3A4028` to define cards — no drop shadows. Balanced density: not crowded, not airy — like a full menu board with room to read.

**Signature element**
The wheat stalk logo drawn as a single fine-line white illustration, as if a careful hand chalked it. It appears *only* on the order confirmation screen — earned, not decorative.

**Where it could go wrong**
A dark UI at night sounds ideal, but if the customer's screen brightness is already low next to a sleeping partner, dark-on-dark demands squinting. The bigger trap is texture: any chalk-grain CSS filter (a browser technique for adding visual effects) or stock overlay will make this look like a free WordPress theme the moment a developer touches it. The restraint must be contractual.

---

## Direction 2 — Kraft Stamp

**Concept:** The inside of a wax-lined French bakery box — the brand *is* the box: unbleached paper, a single two-color rubber stamp, nothing else. Rooted in the tactile minimalism of a Parisian *boulangerie* (small neighbourhood bread bakery) wrapping a baguette at 7am.

**Typography**
- Display: **Cormorant Garamond** (Google Fonts) — the thinnest weight that still holds at headline sizes. It carries the slight irregularity of French hot-metal printing (type cast from molten metal, giving each letter a slightly uneven edge) without announcing itself as "vintage."
- Text: **Source Serif 4** (Google Fonts) — uses optical sizing (automatically adjusted letterform details at small sizes so thin strokes don't disappear) to stay sharp at 14px on mid-range phones where font rendering is less forgiving.

**Color**

| Role | Hex | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| Background | `#EDE0C8` | Raw kraft — not beige, not tan, not warm grey |
| Surface | `#F8F1E2` | Unbleached paper white for cards |
| Text | `#261A0A` | Near-black with a brown pull, like iron-gall ink |
| Muted text | `#907755` | Faded ink for secondary information |
| Accent | `#B03A22` | Wax-seal red; *only* the primary CTA button and the order confirmation badge |
| Alert | `#1A4A2E` | Deep forest green for "selling out" — unusual for an alert colour, but this is a bakery, not a fire alarm |

**Shape language**
0px radius everywhere — folded cardboard has no curves. Hairline 1px borders in `#C8B898` define cards. Zero shadows. This is the most structured of the three directions.

**Signature element**
The order confirmation shows the wheat-stalk mark printed in red as a single flat stamp impression — the visual equivalent of the baker pressing a rubber stamp on the box before handing it over.

**Where it could go wrong**
Cormorant Garamond is glorious at 48px and genuinely dangerous at 13px. You'll need a hard size floor and must test body copy on a mid-range Android device before committing. The other trap: the moment any rustic illustration, secondary handwritten font, or "artisan" badge joins the layout, this tips irreversibly into Etsy-farmer's-market territory. One voice, no guests.

---

## Direction 3 — Recipe Tin

**Concept:** A typed index card inside a recipe tin that's been passed down — the typewriter keys didn't all strike at the same depth, the green pen has added a note in the margin. Rooted in a specific domestic object rather than a style.

**Typography**
- Display: **Fraunces** (Google Fonts) — a variable optical serif (a single font file containing a range of weights and optical styles that shift smoothly between them) designed explicitly to feel "wonky and wonderful." It has the warmth of old type without faking it.
- Text: **Literata** (Google Fonts) — designed for sustained reading on OLED screens (displays that can produce true black by turning pixels fully off, which sharpens the contrast between text and background); warm, bookish, forgiving at small sizes.

**Color**

| Role | Hex | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| Background | `#FDFAF2` | Aged paper white — not stark, not yellow |
| Surface | `#F5EFE0` | Index-card cream for product cards |
| Text | `#1A1510` | Deep brown-black ink |
| Muted text | `#78705F` | Pencil grey-brown for secondary info |
| Accent | `#3D6B35` | Your brand's dark green — used *only* for confirmed/checked states and the single primary action button |
| Alert | `#A83C1E` | Brick terracotta for low-stock |

**Shape language**
4px radius (a card with worn corners). Soft box shadows (`0 1px 4px rgba(0,0,0,0.10)`) instead of borders — the card lifts slightly from the surface. Airy layout: generous line-height and vertical spacing so the screen never feels like a checkout form.

**Signature element**
Every product card shows its key ingredients in muted text directly under the name — *"Dark rye flour, caraway, sea salt"* — styled like a typed recipe line. It's real information used as a design element. It tells customers what they're ordering and makes the screen feel like your bakery, not a menu app.

**Where it could go wrong**
The airy layout is beautiful on a 390px-wide phone but turns ordering into an endless scroll on a smaller device — customers lose their sense of progress. You'll need a strict information hierarchy and must resist every invitation to add more recipe-card charm (illustrated dividers, a second handwritten font, decorative rules) once building starts. The restraint is the whole point.

---

## Recommendation

Start with **Direction 3 — Recipe Tin.**

It's the only direction rooted in all three of your own references simultaneously: the recipe card is the literal concept, the dark green accent is your existing brand, and the ingredient-line card detail borrows the stamp's economy of means. Fraunces is genuinely unusual in food-ordering interfaces — I've never seen it used there, which is the point — and Literata will hold up under the real test: a tired person, low brightness, ordering at 10pm on a three-year-old phone.

# TherapyDesk — Spec
*(working name — replace when you have one)*

---

## 1. One-liner
A private booking and session-notes tool for a solo licensed therapist: clients sign up, pay per session, and the therapist keeps confidential clinical records they can never see.

---

## 2. Users & Roles

| Role | What they can do | What they must NEVER be able to do |
|---|---|---|
| **Therapist** | Log in; set and remove availability slots; view all bookings; cancel any booking; view all client profiles and intake forms; write, edit, and read session notes; view full payment history | Share or expose session notes to any client or third party |
| **Client** | Create an account; complete intake form; browse and book available slots; pay per session; view their own bookings; cancel their own bookings; view their own profile and submitted intake form (read-only) | Read session notes; view another client's data; avoid a cancellation charge after the 24-hour window has passed |

---

## 3. The Core Loop

1. Client creates an account (name, email, phone, password).
2. Client completes the intake form before they can book.
3. Client browses available slots and selects one.
4. Client pays the session fee; payment must succeed for the booking to be confirmed.
5. Client receives an SMS reminder 24 hours before the session and another 1 hour before.
6. Client attends the session.
7. Therapist writes and saves confidential session notes against that appointment.

---

## 4. Features — V1 (must ship)

**Client Booking**
*As a client, I want to see available slots and reserve one, so that I can schedule a therapy session.*
- [ ] Calendar view shows only slots the therapist has marked available.
- [ ] A slot already held by another booking does not appear.
- [ ] Booking is not confirmed until payment succeeds (see Per-Session Payment).
- [ ] Confirmed booking appears immediately in the client's My Bookings list.
- [ ] Therapist sees the new booking immediately on their Dashboard.
- [ ] Empty state: "No slots available right now — please check back soon."

---

**Per-Session Payment**
*As a client, I want to pay for my session at the time of booking, so that my appointment is secured.*
- [ ] Client sees the session fee clearly before entering payment details.
- [ ] Payment must succeed before any booking record is created.
- [ ] A payment confirmation is shown on screen after success.
- [ ] On failure the screen shows: *"Payment was not completed. Please try again or use a different card."* No booking is created and the slot stays available.
- [ ] Therapist's Payment History lists every payment: date, client name, amount, and refund status.

---

**Intake Form**
*As a therapist, I want every new client to complete an intake form (including medical history and medications) before their first session, so that I have the clinical context I need.*
- [ ] After sign-up, the client is taken directly to the intake form and cannot reach the booking screen until it is submitted.
- [ ] Required fields: full name, date of birth, emergency contact name and phone, presenting concerns (free text), medical history (free text), current medications (free text).
- [ ] Submitting with any required field empty shows a field-level error; submission is blocked.
- [ ] After submission the client can view (but not edit) their intake form on their Profile screen.
- [ ] Intake form is visible to the therapist from the Client Profile screen.
- [ ] Intake form is never shown on any screen accessible to other clients.

---

**Session Notes**
*As a therapist, I want to write confidential notes after each session, so that I maintain a clinical record.*
- [ ] Each appointment in the therapist's view has a "Write Notes" button; this button does not exist anywhere in the client's view.
- [ ] Notes are linked to the specific appointment and can be written or edited at any time after the appointment is created.
- [ ] Notes field accepts at least 10,000 characters without truncation.
- [ ] Notes are never visible on any client-facing screen — not in My Bookings, Profile, or anywhere else.
- [ ] Therapist sees "No notes yet" for sessions where nothing has been written.

---

**SMS Reminders**
*As a client, I want text reminders before my session, so that I don't forget to attend.*
- [ ] Client receives an SMS 24 hours before the appointment start time.
- [ ] Client receives an SMS 1 hour before the appointment start time.
- [ ] Each SMS states: appointment date, time, and a one-line note about the 24-hour cancellation policy.
- [ ] If either SMS fails to send, the booking remains confirmed and the therapist's Dashboard shows a warning: *"SMS reminder failed for [Client Name] — [date/time]."*

---

**Cancellation Enforcement**
*As a therapist, I want clients who cancel within 24 hours to be charged the full fee, so that my income is protected.*
- [ ] Client can cancel any upcoming booking from My Bookings.
- [ ] Cancellation more than 24 hours before the session: full refund is issued and the slot is freed for rebooking. Client sees: *"Your booking has been cancelled and a full refund is on its way."*
- [ ] Cancellation 24 hours or fewer before the session: no refund. Client sees: *"Per our cancellation policy, this session fee is non-refundable."* Slot is freed for rebooking.
- [ ] Before confirming a late cancellation, client is shown a warning that they will not be refunded, with "Confirm cancellation" and "Go back" options.
- [ ] Therapist can cancel any booking on behalf of a client (e.g. therapist is unavailable); this always issues a full refund.
- [ ] Therapist's Dashboard shows all cancellations with: timestamp, client name, and whether a refund was issued.

---

**Availability Management**
*As a therapist, I want to set and update my available appointment slots, so that clients only book times that work for me.*
- [ ] Therapist can add a slot: date, start time, and duration in minutes.
- [ ] Therapist can delete any slot that has not yet been booked.
- [ ] Attempting to delete a slot that has a confirmed booking shows: *"This slot has a booking. Cancel the booking first."* — and does nothing.
- [ ] All changes to availability appear immediately on the client-facing booking screen.
- [ ] Empty state on the Availability Manager: *"No slots added yet."*

---

## 5. Features — Later (explicitly NOT in V1)

- Recurring / package bookings
- Video or phone call integration
- Secure in-app messaging
- Rescheduling (V1: client cancels and rebooks manually)
- Waitlist for fully-booked periods
- Email reminders (SMS only in V1)
- Insurance billing / superbill generation
- Document uploads (referral letters, prior records)
- Outcome measures or progress tracking
- Multi-therapist / group practice mode
- Two-factor authentication *(strongly recommended before handling health data at scale, but deferred)*

---

## 6. Screens

### Client-facing

| Screen | Purpose | What's on it | Where you can go |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sign Up** | New client creates an account | Name, email, phone, password fields; "Already have an account?" link | → Intake Form (mandatory next step) |
| **Log In** | Returning client authenticates | Email, password; link to Sign Up; password reset link | → My Bookings (if intake form already done) or → Intake Form |
| **Intake Form** | Collect clinical background before first booking | Date of birth, emergency contact name/phone, presenting concerns, medical history, current medications; Submit button | → Book a Session (only after successful submit) |
| **Book a Session** | Browse and select an available slot | Calendar or list of available slots; slot date, time, duration, fee; "Book this slot" button | → Payment |
| **Payment** | Confirm and pay | Session summary (date, time, fee); card details entry; Pay button; on failure: error message + stay on screen | → My Bookings (on success) |
| **My Bookings** | View all client bookings | Upcoming bookings (date, time, Cancel button); past bookings (date, time, status: attended / cancelled); empty state message | → Cancel Booking; → Book a Session |
| **Cancel Booking** | Confirm a cancellation | Slot details; refund eligibility message; "Confirm cancellation" and "Go back" buttons | → My Bookings |
| **Profile** | View and update account details | Name, email, phone (editable); password change; submitted intake form (read-only) | — |

### Therapist-facing

| Screen | Purpose | What's on it | Where you can go |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Therapist Login** | Therapist authenticates | Email, password | → Dashboard |
| **Dashboard** | Daily overview | Today's sessions; upcoming bookings; recent cancellations (with refund status); SMS send failures; quick link to each session's notes | → Session Notes; → Client Profile; → Availability Manager |
| **Availability Manager** | Control bookable slots | List of all slots with status (available / booked); Add slot form (date, time, duration); Delete button (blocked if booked) | → Dashboard |
| **Client List** | Browse all clients | Alphabetical list of all registered clients; search/filter by name | → Client Profile |
